book: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology, 4th ed. (Rizzo)
kicker: Lesson 12 of your course, built from Chapter 12 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What the endocrine system does
teach: The endocrine system controls the body chemically, keeping the internal environment within narrow ranges (homeostasis). It shares this job with the nervous system.
Endocrine glands are ductless: they secrete hormones straight into the bloodstream, which carries them to target organs. Exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) have ducts.
Hormones control cellular respiration, growth and reproduction, water and electrolyte balance, other hormones, behavior, reproductive cycles and growth and development.

items.label: Sweat gland
items.feedback: Has a duct to the skin.

items.label: Salivary gland
items.feedback: Has a duct to the mouth.

steps.title: Negative feedback
teach: Most hormones are controlled by negative feedback, like a thermostat. When a hormone’s level rises, it inhibits the gland that made it, so secretion drops. When the level falls, the inhibition stops and the gland secretes again.
This keeps hormone levels within a narrow range. Thyroid hormone is a good example: high levels inhibit TSH from the pituitary and TRH from the hypothalamus.

act.prompt: In negative feedback, a rising blood level of a hormone:

options.label: Inhibits further secretion from its gland
Causes the gland to secrete even more
Has no effect on the gland

steps.title: Three chemical types of hormones
teach: Modified amino acids: epinephrine and norepinephrine (adrenal medulla), oxytocin and vasopressin (posterior pituitary).
Proteins: insulin (pancreas), growth hormone and the gonad-stimulating hormones (anterior pituitary).
Steroids, which are lipids: cortisol (adrenal cortex), estrogen and testosterone (gonads).

Amino acid and protein hormones bind to receptors on the cell membrane. Steroids diffuse into the cell and bind inside. Steroids can be taken by mouth (like birth control pills); protein hormones such as insulin must be injected because digestion breaks them down.

items.label: Insulin
items.feedback: Protein, so it must be injected.

steps.title: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary
teach: The pituitary is often called the master gland, but the hypothalamus actually controls it. The hypothalamus plays the major role in controlling pituitary secretions.

The infundibulum is the stalk joining the hypothalamus to the pituitary. Hypothalamic neurons make releasing hormones and release-inhibiting hormones that travel through a portal vein to the anterior pituitary. For example, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) tells the anterior pituitary to secrete TSH.

act.prompt: Which part of the brain plays a major role in controlling the pituitary?

steps.title: The anterior pituitary: seven hormones
teach: The pituitary (hypophysis) is pea-sized and sits in the sphenoid bone. It has a larger anterior lobe and a smaller posterior lobe.

Growth hormone (GH) makes cells grow and divide and builds bone and muscle. Too little in childhood causes pituitary dwarfism; too much in childhood causes gigantism; too much after growth stops causes acromegaly.

TSH stimulates the thyroid. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to make cortisol. MSH increases melanin and darkens the skin. FSH develops ovarian follicles (sperm production in males). LH triggers ovulation and progesterone (testosterone in males). Prolactin (LTH) stimulates milk production after delivery.

act.prompt: Match the hormone to its effect.

steps.title: The posterior pituitary: ADH and oxytocin
teach: The posterior lobe stores and releases two hormones made in the hypothalamus.
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, or vasopressin) makes the kidneys reabsorb water, so less is lost in urine. Too little ADH causes diabetes insipidus: 20 to 30 liters of urine a day and severe dehydration.
Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions during childbirth and milk ejection during breastfeeding. It can be given to induce labor.

steps.title: The thyroid gland
teach: The thyroid has two lobes joined by an isthmus, beside the trachea below the larynx. It needs iodine; without enough, it enlarges into a goiter.
It makes thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which regulate metabolism and are needed for growth and nervous system development. It also makes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.

Too little thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism): in children, cretinism (stunted growth and development); in adults, sluggishness and myxedema, an accumulation of fluid in the subcutaneous tissue. Too much (hyperthyroidism): nervousness and high metabolism. Graves’ disease is hyperthyroidism from overproduction of thyroid hormone, often with a goiter and bulging eyes.

act.prompt: Too little or too much thyroid hormone?

steps.title: The parathyroid glands
teach: Four raisin-sized parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid. They secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH, or parathormone).
PTH raises blood calcium: it makes osteoclasts break down bone and release calcium and phosphate, makes the kidneys conserve calcium and helps the intestine absorb it.
Hyperparathyroidism breaks down bone, so the bones become soft and deformed, and can cause kidney stones. Hypoparathyroidism lowers blood calcium and causes cramps and spasms.

items.label: Calcitonin (thyroid)
items.detail: Lowers blood calcium; stores it in bone.

items.label: PTH (parathyroids)
items.detail: Raises blood calcium; releases it from bone.

act.prompt: When blood calcium is too low, which gland releases calcium and phosphate into the blood?

steps.title: The adrenal glands
teach: The adrenal (suprarenal) glands sit on top of the kidneys. Each has two parts that act as separate glands.
The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine (adrenaline) and some norepinephrine, the fight-or-flight hormones. They release glucose and fatty acids for energy and raise heart rate and blood pressure.

The adrenal cortex has three layers. The outer layer secretes mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone, which controls sodium and potassium. The middle layer secretes cortisol (a glucocorticoid), which raises blood glucose and reduces inflammation. The inner layer secretes androgens.
Too little cortex hormone causes Addison’s disease (bronzed skin, low sodium and blood sugar). Too much causes Cushing’s syndrome (high blood sugar, round moon face, fat on the trunk).

act.prompt: Which part of the adrenal gland?

steps.title: The pancreas: insulin and glucagon
teach: The pancreas is both exocrine (digestive juice) and endocrine. Its islets of Langerhans make two hormones that control blood glucose.
Beta cells secrete insulin after a meal. Insulin moves glucose into the liver (stored as glycogen), muscle and fat, lowering blood glucose.
Alpha cells secrete glucagon when glucose falls. Glucagon makes the liver convert stored glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose.
If glucose gets very low, breaking down fat releases ketones and lowers blood pH: acidosis.

mnemonic.explanation: Glucagon raises glucose when it’s "gone"; insulin puts glucose "in" storage.

steps.title: Diabetes mellitus
teach: Diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency in insulin production (or fewer insulin receptors). Blood glucose stays high (hyperglycemia).
Classic signs: glucose in the urine (glycosuria), lots of urine (polyuria), excessive thirst (polydipsia) and intense hunger (polyphagia), with weight loss. Fat breakdown can cause acidosis.
Type 1 is autoimmune, usually starts young and needs insulin (about 10% of cases). Type 2 is the most common (about 90%), usually after 40 and linked to excess weight; diet and exercise are key.
Diabetes insipidus is different: it’s caused by too little ADH.

act.prompt: Match the sign to its term.

steps.title: Gonads, thymus and pineal gland
teach: The testes make testosterone, which develops male structures and secondary sex characteristics. Anabolic steroids are variants of testosterone. The ovaries make estrogen and progesterone, which develop female structures and control the menstrual cycle.
The thymus, in the mediastinum, secretes thymosin, which produces T lymphocytes for immunity. It’s large in children and shrinks with age.

The pineal gland secretes melatonin. Bright light inhibits it; darkness increases it. Melatonin regulates circadian rhythms (sleep-wake cycles). Seasonal affective disorder occurs in people sensitive to overproduction of melatonin in dark winter months; bright light therapy helps.

items.label: Anabolic steroids are variants of it

steps.title: Endocrine disorders review
teach: Use this to keep the disorders straight: gigantism (too much GH in childhood), acromegaly (too much GH after childhood), pituitary dwarfism (too little GH), goiter (enlarged thyroid from lack of iodine), Graves’ disease (too much thyroid hormone), myxedema (too little thyroid hormone in adults), Addison’s disease (too little adrenal cortex hormone), Cushing’s syndrome (too much cortisol), aldosteronism (too much aldosterone, high blood pressure), adrenogenital syndrome (too many adrenal androgens).

act.prompt: Match the disorder to its cause.

items.label: Too much growth hormone after childhood

steps.title: The endocrine system and aging
teach: Growth hormone falls with age, reducing bone and muscle mass and increasing fat. Sex hormones fall in later middle age (menopause in women). Thymosin falls, weakening immunity. Melatonin falls, changing sleep patterns. Regular exercise helps.

act.prompt: Which hormone’s decline with age affects immunity, according to the textbook?

options.label: Insulin
options.feedback: The textbook links thymosin to immunity.

quiz.q: Insulin and growth hormone are examples of ___________________________ hormones.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 lists insulin and growth hormone as protein hormones. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: An accumulation of fluid in subcutaneous tissue is called _______________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says an accumulation of fluid in subcutaneous tissues is called myxedema. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Modified amino acid hormones include _______________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 lists epinephrine and norepinephrine as modified amino acid hormones. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Overproduction of thyroid hormone results in _______________________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says Graves’ disease is a type of hyperthyroidism caused by overproduction of thyroid hormone. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Secretion of ______ from the anterior pituitary increases pigmentation or darkening of the skin.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says melanocyte-stimulating hormone increases melanin, darkening the skin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Testosterone and cortisol are examples of _______________________________ hormones.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 lists cortisol, estrogen and testosterone as steroid hormones. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Excess secretion of growth hormone after childhood results in ______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says excess growth hormone after childhood, when bones have stopped growing, results in acromegaly. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Stimulation of uterine muscle contractions during childbirth is triggered by ______________________ .
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says oxytocin stimulates contraction of the uterine muscles in the late stages of childbirth. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: In the pancreas, insulin is secreted by cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says beta cells secrete insulin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The release of ___________________, stimulates the liver to convert the stored glycogen into glucose.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says glucagon stimulates the liver to convert stored glycogen into glucose. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Excessive thirst is called _____________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 defines polydipsia as excessive thirst. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Anabolic steroids are variants of the male sex hormone _________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says anabolic steroids are variants of the male sex hormone testosterone. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Following childbirth, _______________________ stimulates milk production in the mammary glands.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says prolactin stimulates milk production in the mammary glands following delivery. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The outer layer of the adrenal cortex secretes a group of hormones called _______________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says the outer layer of the adrenal cortex secretes mineralocorticoid hormones. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The common disorder ______________________ is caused by a deficiency in insulin production.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency in insulin production. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The hormones insulin and glucagon are produced by the ____________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says the pancreatic islets produce insulin and glucagon. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Secretion of _________________________ from the anterior pituitary stimulates ovulation in the ovary.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says luteinizing hormone stimulates ovulation in the ovary. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The ______________________ gland, also known as the hypophysis, is divided into two lobes.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says the pituitary gland, also called the hypophysis, is divided into two lobes. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Too much secretion of adrenal cortex hormones can lead to ________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says too much secretion from the adrenal cortex can lead to Cushing’s syndrome. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The ___________________ gland stimulates the release of calcium and phosphate ions into the blood when calcium levels become too low.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says parathyroid hormone releases calcium and phosphate ions into the blood and raises blood calcium to normal. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Inadequate amounts of iodine in the diet leads to an enlarged thyroid gland, known as a(n) __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says that without enough iodine, the thyroid gland enlarges, forming a goiter. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Circadian rhythms are regulated by __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says studies indicate melatonin regulates circadian rhythms. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Seasonal affective disorder occurs in individuals who are sensitive to overproduction of ___________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says seasonal affective disorder occurs in individuals sensitive to an overproduction of melatonin. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The release of ________ from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete TSH.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says the hypothalamus produces thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete TSH. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Hyperparathyroidism results in the softening and deformation of the _______________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says hyperparathyroidism breaks down bone matrix, so bones become soft and deformed. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are commonly referred to as the fight-or-flight hormones.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says epinephrine and norepinephrine are commonly called the fight-or-flight hormones. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The exocrine glands are ductless glands that secrete hormone directly into the bloodstream.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood. Exocrine glands have ducts. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Negative feedback occurs when the increasing blood level of a hormone inhibits its continued secretion from its source endocrine gland.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says that when a hormone reaches a certain level, the gland that secreted it is inhibited (negative feedback). Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: The thalamus plays a major role in controlling secretions from the pituitary gland.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says the hypothalamus, not the thalamus, plays a major role in controlling secretions from the pituitary gland. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.

quiz.q: A lowering of blood pH is called acidosis.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 12 says a lowering of blood pH is a condition known as acidosis. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 12.
